sections.body_en:
When the soldiers returned from the war against Midian with abundant spoils, including food vessels made of metal, Elazar the Kohen instructed them to kasher the food vessels from the non-kosher foods that the Midianites had eaten in them, as it is stated (Bamidbar 31:21-23): "This is the statute of the Torah which the Lord commanded Moshe. Only the gold, and the silver, the copper, the iron, the tin and the lead – everything that may go through fire you shall pass through fire and it shall be clean; nevertheless it shall be purified with the water of sprinkling; and all that may not go through fire you shall pass through water." From here the Sages learned that the kashering of vessels is according to the manner in which they absorbed – 'as it absorbs, so it expels' (ke-bol'o kakh polto): vessels used with fire, such as skewers and baking pans, are kashered by libun (heating to a glow) in fire; vessels used for cooking are kashered by hagala (purging) in boiling water; and vessels used with cold food are kashered by hadaḥa (rinsing) in water (Avoda Zara 75b). Thus there are three types of kashering: libun, hagala and hadaḥa (above 31:1 we learned that to kasher non-Jews' vessels, they must also be immersed).

Let us explain further: a vessel that was used with foods that are not hot, since the food residue sticks to the vessel only loosely, can be removed by washing in cold water, and this is hadaḥa. But if the use was through cooking, the tastes in the cooked food stick to and are absorbed in the vessel, and only boiling water can expel them, and this is hagala. And if the use was with ur, that is, with fire, as with skewers or baking pans, since there are no liquids there to soften the adhesion of the foods to the walls, the tastes are absorbed into the vessel with great force, and therefore boiling water does not have the power to expel them from the walls of the vessel; rather, they must be kashered in the manner in which they absorbed – with ur, that is, by libun.

Apparently, when the Sages spoke of the tastes absorbed in a vessel, they also meant tastes that had stuck firmly to its walls through cooking, to the point that they were considered absorbed in it. For in the past, when there were no pipes carrying water to every home, and the method of mass-producing soap that effectively removes fats and dirt from vessels had not yet been found, and the surfaces of vessels were rough, without hagala in boiling water that dissolved the fats stuck to the vessels, residues of the foods cooked in them would generally remain stuck to the walls of the vessels (below note 6). It follows, then, that the instruction of the mitzva to kasher metal vessels in the manner in which they absorbed is also directed at the tastes that stuck to their walls. And although even after hagala some slight residue of the previous food may still remain on the walls of the vessel, since the vessel was purged as the Torah commanded, and this hagala removed most of the tastes that stuck to the vessel to the point that their taste could not be perceived, they are as if nullified and no longer contain any prohibition.1

notes_en.en: It is implied by the Rishonim that a fatty layer of food residue was stuck to the vessels that were purged, and hagala in boiling water would remove it, since fats dissolve in heat and with the help of the water are washed away and separated from the walls of the vessels. Therefore the Ra'ah wrote (Bedek Ha-bayit 4:4) not to purge many vessels in the same water, out of concern "that the filth will increase and the power of the water will be nullified and the form of the water will pass away; and this is very correct, and it is visible to the eye that the boiling water polishes the vessel, and as long as it remains there it becomes cleaner and more scoured." This implies that hagala cleaned the outer layers stuck to the vessel. And similarly it is explained in the Ran (Ḥullin 44a in the pages of the Rif) and in the Or Zaru'a (2:256). And so wrote the Ohel Mo'ed (Sha'ar Ha-Pesaḥ, Derekh 3, Netiv 6), that one must clean the vessels before hagala "in order to reduce the fat in them," which shows that the cleaning reduced the adhering fat but did not remove it completely. And the Me'iri wrote (Avoda Zara 75b) that food residues that do not come off in hagala do not render forbidden because they are "like what they said regarding immersion, that a small amount that one does not care about does not interpose."

sections.title_en: Forbidden Tastes in Vessels Render Cooked Foods Forbidden
sections.body_en:
In addition to the prohibition of using vessels in which non-kosher food was cooked and which were not properly kashered, if kosher food was cooked in them, the food becomes forbidden. This is because the taste of the food cooked in a vessel sticks to and is absorbed in its walls, and if, after non-kosher food was cooked in a pot, kosher food is cooked in it, the non-kosher taste will come out of the walls and be absorbed in the kosher food. We regard the walls as if they are full of the forbidden taste, and since the contents of pots almost never amount to sixty times the thickness of their walls, whenever food is cooked in a pot that absorbed a forbidden taste, everything cooked in the pot becomes forbidden. The same law applies to a pot in which milk was cooked and afterwards meat was cooked in it: since the meat dish is not sixty times the thickness of the dairy walls, the meat dish becomes forbidden.

Why do we regard the wall as if it is full of the forbidden taste? Because this is a doubt that cannot be resolved, for it is impossible to estimate how much taste stuck to and was absorbed in the walls, and how much taste they expel. Some vessels absorb more and some absorb less. Earthenware vessels absorb a lot, wooden vessels less, and metal vessels still less. Among earthenware vessels there are also differences: there are porous ones whose absorption is great, and dense ones whose absorption is lesser; new ones absorb a lot, and old ones absorb little. Likewise, there are cooked foods whose taste is concentrated and strong, so that one gram of it is equivalent to ten grams of an ordinary dish, to the point that sometimes the taste coming out of the vessels is as strong as the volume of their walls. And since this is a constant doubt whose limits cannot be determined, and a permanent state of doubt is a state that undermines the boundaries of the prohibition, the halakha was ruled that, in order to leave the realm of doubt, one must be stringent to the furthest extreme and regard all the walls of the pot as if they are full of the taste of the non-kosher dish; and since the dish is not sixty times the volume of the walls, the dish becomes forbidden.

Not only that, but if another dish is afterwards cooked in that same pot, it too becomes forbidden. For there is a doubt: perhaps in the first cooking the forbidden taste was not expelled, whereas in the second cooking the forbidden taste was expelled. And since we cannot estimate how much was expelled the first time and how much the second time, one must be stringent to the furthest extreme and calculate each time as if all the taste absorbed in the walls was expelled on that occasion.

The safety rules we have learned are intended for a situation in which we have no possibility of ascertaining the taste of the dish, for a Jew cannot check the taste of the dish, lest it turn out that it contains a forbidden taste and he will have eaten forbidden food. But if there is a reliable non-Jew there who tasted the dish and said that the forbidden taste is not perceptible in it, the dish is kosher. However, since tastes are elusive, it is generally customary not to rely on a non-Jew, but rather to determine the law according to the safety rules we have learned (below 34:4-5).2

notes_en.en:
In Ḥullin 97b it is explained that by rabbinic law it is forbidden to eat kaḥal (an animal's udder) without removing all the milk residue from it, and if this was not done and it was put into a meat dish, we must estimate as if it is all milk, and sixty times its volume is required. Most Rishonim learned from this that the same law applies to a vessel: as long as there is no kafila (a non-Jewish cook) to check the taste of the dish, since there is no possibility of estimating the matter, the estimate is according to the volume of the walls of the vessel. This is the opinion of the Ramban, Rashba, Rosh, Sefer Ha-teruma, Ra'ah, Roke'aḥ, Ritva, Ran and others, and so it was ruled in the SA (98:4; 94:1).
However, according to the Ra'avad and Rid, if kosher food was cooked in a non-kosher pot, the estimate is not according to the thickness of its walls; rather, one makes a good estimate leaning toward stringency of how much taste came out of the non-kosher pot into the dish. And this is also the opinion of the Ittur, Eshkol and Me'orot, and Rabbeinu Yeruḥam inclined to this. (According to the Ra'avad, whenever it is possible to extract the forbidden taste from it, one estimates according to the taste absorbed in it. And according to the Rid, whenever the prohibition came from elsewhere, one estimates its quantity.) In practice, almost all the Aḥaronim ruled according to the stringent opinion, and some wrote that one should not even combine the lenient opinion to create a double doubt and be lenient (Pri Megadim, Yad Yehuda). The Ginat Veradim ruled like the lenient authorities, and the Torot Emet was lenient in a pressing situation. The Rashakh combined the lenient opinion to create a double doubt for leniency. The Radbaz inclined to this, and so wrote Yabi'a Omer (vol. 8, YD 4).

sections.title_en: Ben Yomo and Eino Ben Yomo; Intentional and Unintentional
sections.body_en:
A vessel in which non-kosher food was cooked is forbidden for use forever, and only after it undergoes kashering is it permitted to use it (SA 122:2). However, what we learned, that the non-kosher taste absorbed in the walls of the vessel renders forbidden what is cooked in the vessel, applies on condition that the vessel is 'ben yomo' (literally, "of its day"), that is, within twenty-four hours from when non-kosher food was cooked in it. For until then, the non-kosher tastes that were absorbed in and stuck to the vessel can still impart a good taste to the dish and render it forbidden. But after a full day has passed, the tastes absorbed in and stuck to the vessel become spoiled, and they can no longer render forbidden what is cooked in the vessel (SA 103:5). When there is a doubt whether a full day has passed over the pot, the pot is regarded as one over which a full day has passed, in accordance with the rule: 'Ordinary vessels are not ben yomam' (SA 122:7).

If they knew that the pot was non-kosher and nevertheless cooked in it deliberately, even though a full day had passed over it and the taste coming out of it is spoiled, the Sages imposed a penalty and forbade the food to the one who cooked and to all those for whom he cooked; only for others, for whom the dish was not cooked, is it permitted to eat it.

Thus the law of the dish is determined by two questions. The first: was the vessel 'ben yomo'? If it was 'ben yomo,' the dish is forbidden to everyone. If the vessel was not ben yomo, the second question arises: was the cooking done intentionally? If intentionally, the dish is forbidden to all those for whom it was cooked and permitted to others; and if unintentionally, the dish is permitted to everyone.3

notes_en.en:
It is explained in the Talmud (Avoda Zara 67b; 75b-76a) that the Tanna'im disagreed regarding a non-kosher vessel that is not ben yomo (in which the absorbed taste is spoiled). According to R. Meir and other Tanna'im and Amora'im, a taste that imparts a spoiled flavor (noten ta'am li-fgam) renders forbidden, and therefore the dish cooked in it is forbidden. According to R. Shimon and other Tanna'im and Amora'im, noten ta'am li-fgam is permitted, and therefore the dish cooked in it is permitted. The halakha follows R. Shimon that noten ta'am li-fgam is permitted (below 34:7). However, even according to R. Shimon it is forbidden to use a non-kosher vessel that is not ben yomo without kashering, for the Sages decreed that vessels that are not ben yomam must be kashered, lest people use them while they are ben yomam. So it is explained in our version of the Talmud, Avoda Zara 76a, and this is the opinion of most Rishonim.
And some hold that even according to R. Shimon there is a Torah obligation to kasher vessels that are not ben yomam, even though in his opinion they do not render forbidden the dishes cooked in them, because this is what the Torah decreed (the Ramban, Avoda Zara 67a, explained that the Torah so decreed lest people use vessels that are ben yomam, and the Ra'avan explained that it is because it is forbidden to nullify Torah prohibitions). In addition to the Ramban and Ra'avan, this is also the opinion of the Ra'avya (Pesaḥim 464), Radbaz (6, §2205), Mor U-ketzi'a (introduction to OḤ, part 2) and the Netziv (Ha'amek She'ela, Matot 137:2). Thus, the dispute between R. Shimon and R. Meir is narrowed, for both agree that even after a full day, by Torah law a vessel in which non-kosher food was cooked must be kashered, and their entire dispute concerns a case after the fact, when someone mistakenly cooked in a vessel that is not ben yomo: according to R. Meir the food is forbidden because even a spoiled taste renders forbidden, and according to R. Shimon the food is kosher, for noten ta'am li-fgam is permitted.
We also find an intermediate opinion between R. Shimon and R. Meir, which is the opinion of the Sages (Pesaḥim 44b), who hold that although as a rule the halakha follows R. Shimon that noten ta'am li-fgam is permitted, regarding vessels we learned an extra stringency in the Torah, that even a spoiled taste absorbed in or stuck to vessels renders forbidden.
Returning to the halakha: as we learned, the halakha follows R. Shimon, and if one cooked in a non-kosher pot that is not ben yomo, the dish is permitted. But all this is on condition that the cooking was done unintentionally; but if the cook knew that the vessel required kashering and transgressed and cooked in it deliberately, even though the pot is not ben yomo, the Sages imposed a penalty and forbade the food to the cook and to those for whom he cooked (Radbaz 3:617; Knesset Ha-gedola YD 122, Hagahot Ha-tur 26). Some Aḥaronim were lenient even for one who cooks deliberately (Tiferet Le-Moshe, Maharam Schick, Shem Aryeh, Igrot Moshe and others). But in practice one should be stringent, for this is the opinion of the Rishonim: Rashba, Ritva and others. And so wrote other Aḥaronim, among them: Binyamin Ze'ev, Kol Eliyahu, Pri Megadim, Beit Shlomo, Zivḥei Tzedek, Yabi'a Omer 8, YD 14; and see Harḥavot.
According to Rashi, Rabbeinu Tam and Maharam Ḥalava, once a night has passed over the vessel it is already considered not ben yomo, and its taste is spoiled and does not render forbidden the dish cooked in it. According to most poskim, only after a full day is the taste spoiled, and this is the opinion of the Ri, Rashbam, Sefer Ha-teruma, Rosh, Tur and SA 103:5.

sections.body_en:
The rule we learned, that vessels are kashered according to the manner of their use, was stated in the Torah regarding metal vessels, as it is stated (Bamidbar 31:22-23): "Only the gold, and the silver, the copper, the iron, the tin and the lead – everything that may go through fire you shall pass through fire… and all that may not go through fire you shall pass through water."

But earthenware vessels, which were cheap and widespread in ancient times, cannot be kashered by hagala or libun. This is because earthenware is full of pores and its absorption is great, and hagala does not have the power to extract from it everything it absorbed. As it is stated (Vayikra 6:21): "But the earthenware vessel in which it is boiled shall be broken; and if it was boiled in a copper vessel, it shall be scoured and rinsed in water." That is, the vessel in which the meat of the sacrifice is cooked absorbs its tastes, and since after the end of the time for eating the meat of the sacrifice, what remains of it (notar) is forbidden to eat, the tastes absorbed in the vessel also become forbidden. The Torah instructed that if the meat of the sacrifice was cooked in a copper vessel, it is kashered by hagala, but if it was cooked in an earthenware vessel, there is no possibility of kashering it, for it never fully rids itself of its absorption, and it must be broken so that people do not mistakenly use it. From this the Sages learned regarding other prohibitions that whenever an earthenware vessel absorbed a forbidden taste, it cannot be kashered.4

In principle, it can be kashered by libun, since libun burns up the earthenware vessel together with the taste absorbed in it. But since an earthenware vessel is liable to crack in the fire, there is concern that one who comes to kasher it by libun will not heat it properly, because he will be anxious about it lest it crack; therefore the Sages forbade kashering an earthenware vessel by libun. However, it can be kashered by putting it into a kiln, and if it survives the intense fire there and does not crack, it is like a newly made vessel. There is no concern that it will not be heated properly in the kiln, because the fire in the kiln burns with great intensity and cannot be weakened (Pesaḥim 30b; Tosafot s.v. "Ha-torah"; SA OḤ 451:1).

notes_en.en: In the Yerushalmi (Terumot 11:4) it is explained that an earthenware vessel in which rabbinic teruma was cooked can be kashered by hagala three times. The Rash, Semag and Me'iri wrote that this is the law for any earthenware vessel that absorbed a rabbinic prohibition. And the Ittur added (part 2, Sha'ar 1, page 14c) that even if a Torah prohibition was cooked in the earthenware vessel, since after a full day its taste becomes spoiled, the obligation to extract its taste is consequently rabbinic, and therefore it can be kashered by hagala three times. On the other hand, according to Rabbeinu Simḥa, Or Zaru'a, Hagahot Asheri and SA 113:16, hagala three times is effective only for an earthenware vessel that originally absorbed a rabbinic prohibition that has no basis in Torah law, such as teruma in our times. And according to the Ramban and Ra'ah, they were lenient only with rabbinic teruma, but from other rabbinic prohibitions an earthenware vessel may not be kashered by hagala three times. In practice, when there are additional reasons to be lenient, we combine the opinion of the Ittur and kasher by hagala three times. When performing hagala three times, some wrote that the water should be changed each time (Derisha 121:6; Maḥatzit Ha-shekel; Ḥazon Ish; Ḥazon Ovadia). And some hold that it need not be changed (Rashal; see Hora'a Berura 121 in the Issur Ve-heter He-arokh).

sections.body_en:
A dispute arose in the period of the Rishonim regarding glass vessels. Some say that since glass is smooth and hard, even if hot foods were in it, it does not absorb their taste. Therefore, if glass vessels were used for forbidden foods, it is sufficient to clean them well in order to use them for kosher foods (Ra'avya, Rosh, Rashba, Ran, SA OḤ 451:26). On the other hand, some say that since glass is made from sand, like earthenware vessels, even if in practice glass vessels do not absorb, their law is like that of earthenware vessels, which cannot be remedied: if boiling non-kosher foods were placed in them, there is no possibility of kashering them, and they must be thrown away or given to a non-Jew (R. Yeḥiel, Semag, Rabbeinu Peretz, Terumat Ha-deshen).

And some took the middle path, and in their opinion the law of glass vessels is like that of metal vessels: if they were used for boiling non-kosher foods, they must be kashered by hagala in boiling water (Rambam, Or Zaru'a and Shibolei Ha-leket).

In general, those of Sephardic descent inclined to the lenient opinion, and some even customarily eat hot meat and dairy foods from the same glass plates, while taking care to clean them well between meat and dairy. On the other hand, those of Ashkenazic descent inclined to the stringent opinion, and some even ruled to throw away glass vessels that were mistakenly used with boiling non-kosher food, or once for meat and once for dairy. However, when one looks more deeply, one finds that most of the Jewish people customarily followed the middle path. For it is reasonable that the Sephardic custom of being lenient with glass vessels was mainly with a keli sheni (secondary vessel), because glass vessels in the past were liable to break when cooked on a fire. And even with a keli sheni, many of Sephardic descent were stringent and did not use the same vessels for meat and dairy. On the other hand, most Ashkenazic poskim, who incline to stringency, agree that after the fact, if non-kosher food was cooked in a glass vessel, it can be kashered by hagala in accordance with the intermediate opinion.

Thus, the custom of most of the Jewish people is to follow the middle path: to separate between meat and dairy glass vessels, and to kasher vessels in which the other kind or non-kosher food was mistakenly cooked, in the way that is practiced with metal vessels. And so it is proper to instruct all Jews, as will be explained below (halakhot 7-9) regarding metal vessels.5

notes_en.en:
There are three opinions among the Rishonim: a) The lenient authorities hold that glass vessels do not need kashering by hagala but only cleaning, and this is the opinion of Tosafot, Ra'avya, Eshkol, Rashba, Rosh, Ran and Rashbatz.
b) The stringent authorities hold that there is no possibility of kashering them by hagala, because their law is like that of earthenware vessels; this is the opinion of Rabbeinu Yeḥiel of Paris, Rabbeinu Peretz, Hagahot Maimoniyot, Terumat Ha-deshen, Agur and Maharil. c) According to the intermediate opinion, their law is like that of metal vessels, which require hagala; this is the opinion of the Or Zaru'a, Shibolei Ha-leket, and Ra'ah (as long as there is no concern that they will break in the hagala). And so it appears from the Rambam (Hilkhot Ma'akhalot Asurot 17:3). At the root of the dispute, it appears that even the stringent authorities agree that glass vessels do not absorb a perceptible taste, and after the fact the food cooked in them should not be forbidden. Nevertheless, their opinion is that since glass is made from sand like earthenware, glass vessels cannot be kashered, like earthenware vessels. And according to the intermediate opinion, they must be purged like metal vessels, because the obligation of hagala does not depend on absorption, as explained below in halakhot 7-8. Sephardic custom: in SA OḤ 451:26 he ruled according to the lenient opinion, to use glass vessels on Pesaḥ without kashering. The Pri Ḥadash, Sdei Ḥemed and others wrote that this is the Sephardic custom. But it is reasonable that in practice they were lenient in this only with a keli sheni, which does not cook (below 35:4), because glass vessels in the past were not strong enough to cook in them as a keli rishon. Thus, at most the custom to permit concerned pouring (irui) from a keli rishon, which we are stringent to regard as cooking to the depth of a peel (kedei klipa) (below 35, note 3), and with glass vessels they were lenient that it does not cook. In addition, many immigrants from the communities of North Africa and the East testify that in practice they were very careful not to use the same vessels for meat and dairy even as a keli sheni. And it is possible that even the lenient authorities were in practice lenient in this only in a case of special need, when vessels were lacking. In practice, some Sephardic poskim inclined to be stringent (Knesset Ha-gedola, Or Le-Tzion, Rav Ḥayim David Halevi). Some ruled that by law one must be stringent with a keli rishon (Rav Pe'alim 3, OḤ 29; Rav David Shloush in Responsa Ḥemda Genuza 16; Rav Kafiḥ; and Rav Eliyahu). On the other hand, many wrote to permit ab initio using even a keli rishon for meat and dairy (Yabi'a Omer vol. 4, OḤ 41:4; YD 5; Netivei Am; Shemesh U-magen; Olat Yitzḥak). In my humble opinion, it is more proper not to use the same vessels for meat and dairy, because apparently in practice the Sephardic communities did not customarily permit this throughout the generations, and this leniency contradicts the other customs of separation accepted among the Jewish people. However, one whose family custom follows the lenient approach of using the same glass vessels for hot meat and dairy may continue their custom; but if there are relatives in his family who customarily are stringent, it is good to take them into consideration.
Ashkenazic custom: the Rema (OḤ 451:26) was stringent not to kasher glass vessels for Pesaḥ by hagala, and after the fact, if one cleaned them, a hot dish placed in them should not be forbidden (Darkhei Moshe 19; Taz 30). And according to the Magen Avraham 49, one may be lenient after the fact only after kashering by hagala, and so wrote the Ḥok Ya'akov 68, Shulḥan Arukh Ha-Rav 73, Mekor Ḥayim 46, and the Maharsham. Some ruled to purge them three times (Tzitz Eliezer 9:26, based on Rav Frank; see above note 4). And many wrote that only regarding ḥametz were they stringent, but from other prohibitions it is permitted to kasher them by hagala. So wrote the Maharam of Brisk, Seridei Esh, Beit Avi, and Minḥat Yitzḥak. And according to She'ilat Ya'avetz 1:67, by law it is possible to kasher glass vessels by rinsing, and only because of the stringency of ḥametz did they customarily not use them; and so wrote the Beit Leḥem Yehuda, Ḥamudei Daniel and Yad Yehuda.
Since there are differences of custom even among the poskim of Sephardic and Ashkenazic descent, and apparently in practice most Jewish communities ruled according to the intermediate approach, I have written for everyone according to the intermediate opinion. See Harḥavot.

sections.body_en:
A question has arisen in our day regarding metal vessels. It is clear that the Sages of the Mishna and Talmud, the Rishonim and the Aḥaronim, regarded metal vessels as absorbing and expelling tastes, and there is no doubt that this is what they actually perceived. Therefore, it was ruled that if non-kosher meat is cooked in a metal pot, the pot absorbs non-kosher tastes, and if a kosher dish is cooked in it before it is kashered by hagala, even though the pot was cleaned well, sometimes the taste of non-kosher meat would be perceived in the dish. Therefore, if there was a reliable non-Jew there who tasted the dish and found that it had no non-kosher taste, they declared the dish kosher. But if there was no reliable non-Jew there, they established that one must be stringent and regard the walls as if they are full of taste, all of which was expelled into the dish; and since the dish is not sixty times the thickness of the walls, the dish is forbidden (as explained in halakha 2). Certainly this stringency was based on the reality the Sages knew, that even after the metal pot was cleaned well, the taste of the dish previously cooked in it could sometimes be perceived in the dish.

On the other hand, people today know that after pots are cleaned properly, not a trace of the taste of the previous dish remains in them, and no one can perceive the taste of the dish previously cooked in them. Various studies have also shown that the absorption of metal and glass vessels is so slight (one part in tens of thousands) that it is impossible to perceive any taste from it. The question is: what has changed in recent generations?

Apparently, the reason for the change lies in a number of technological developments. First, in the past it was not possible to cast metals uniformly (in a vacuum), which created holes through which tastes penetrated into the thickness of the wall. Perhaps the metals were also less pure, and the alloy in them absorbed tastes. Second, in the past the surfaces of vessels were rougher, and consequently it was harder to remove the food residue from them. Third, a significant part of the taste remaining in the vessels after cooking came from the fat that stuck to them, and these tastes were also considered absorbed in the vessel, since they became one with the walls and subordinate to them. Following the development of dish soap less than a hundred years ago, and the connection of homes to running water, it is possible, with water and soap and a scouring cloth, to remove the fats and dirt stuck to the vessel.6

notes_en.en:
It is widely known today that one cannot perceive the tastes expelled from metal vessels. To substantiate this knowledge, I asked those who attend my classes to check meticulously whether they succeed in perceiving the tastes expelled from vessels, or more precisely, whether they succeed in perceiving in a dish the taste of the dish previously cooked in the pot. Over several years, hundreds of men and women followed this, conducting various experiments, and not one was found who succeeded in perceiving the taste of the previous dish cooked in a metal pot after it had been cleaned with soap in the usual way. Even when an extremely spicy dish was cooked, after the pot was cleaned, someone who did not know about it could not perceive in the next dish the spicy taste of what was previously cooked in the pot. There were indeed cases in which people perceived traces of a sort of unclear previous taste or smell, but when they tried to reproduce these sensations, it turned out that this happened because the vessel had not been cleaned well, usually after cleaning by children. But even in those cases, they did not perceive an actual taste of the previous food. Likewise, even expert chefs in luxury restaurants do not detect any taste remaining from previous cooking after the vessel has been properly cleaned with soap, and therefore they use the same vessels for different dishes. This was also found in scientific studies: in Teḥumin 34, pp. 113-129, in the article by Rav Yair Frank and Rav Dr. Dror Fixler, the results of studies about metal and glass vessels were summarized, according to which the absorption of these vessels is minute, to the point that there is no possibility of perceiving its taste.
But it is clear that the testimony of the Sages and poskim is reliable, and in the past they perceived tastes expelled from vessels. Therefore, an explanation for the change must be found. Apparently, a number of technological developments caused the change. First, according to what we know today, even in the past tastes were not actually absorbed into the metals, for unlike earthenware and wood, metal materials of all kinds have no pores through which taste-bearing substances can penetrate into the thickness of the vessel, because taste molecules are much larger than the spaces between the particles of which the various metals are composed. However, since in the past there was no technological possibility of casting metals in a vacuum, air holes sometimes remained in them that could take in tastes. The composition of the metal alloy also included additional materials, which may have absorbed tastes. Second, the surfaces of the vessels were slightly rough, and food residue stuck to them more than to the smooth vessels of our day. Third, the difficulty in cleaning vessels stems from the fact that water does not bond with oil, and since the food residues that stick to the vessels are fatty, water has difficulty bonding with them and removing them. The special quality of soap is that it is composed of molecules that bond with both oil and water, and in this way it can help remove fats. Already thousands of years ago people knew how to make soap by cooking animal fat with ash, and they also used the borit plant for cleaning purposes, but the result was far from the result of our soap. In 1790 the Frenchman Leblanc developed a method that improved the way soap was produced industrially for the masses. But this was still a soap of low effectiveness. About ninety years ago the way was opened to produce effective dish soap through the development of synthetic detergents. All this, together with the connection of homes to running water, significantly improved our ability to clean vessels, to the point that in practice the tastes that stuck to them are not perceived.
In any case, before all these inventions and improvements, even after serious cleaning efforts, a thin layer of food residue that transmitted tastes almost always remained on the wall of the vessel. And since the liquids in this layer evaporated, the taste substances remained there in high concentration, to the point that the Rishonim estimated, based on reality, that sometimes their taste is equivalent to the thickness of the walls (above note 2). And since this is a thin layer exposed to the air, it rots and spoils quickly, to the point that the Sages estimated that if the vessel is not ben yomo, it is already clear that the tastes that stuck to its walls have spoiled (above halakha 3). Incidentally, according to this explanation it is understood how hagala and libun are effective for kashering vessels and removing tastes, for in hagala the heat of the boiling water dissolves the fats, and thus they are expelled and separated from the vessels. And the heat of libun dissolves the fats and burns them.

sections.body_en:
Some argue that since it has become clear that metal vessels do not absorb and expel tastes, according to those who permit using glass vessels for boiling-hot meat and dairy by cleaning alone, one should also permit using metal pots and cutlery for boiling-hot meat and dairy by cleaning alone. Likewise, it would be permitted to use a pot in which non-kosher meat was cooked after cleaning it well. Not only that, but some argue that even the Rishonim who were stringent regarding glass vessels, had they known with certainty that they do not absorb and expel tastes, would have agreed with those who permit, because the entire basis of the prohibition regarding vessels is only the taste absorbed in them. And if in practice the taste is not absorbed in them, it is sufficient to clean them, and there is no need to kasher them by hagala.7

On the other hand, almost all rabbis hold in practice that one must kasher a vessel in which non-kosher food was cooked, and likewise one must kasher a dairy pot in which meat was cooked, or vice versa. For since it has been the custom among the Jewish people for generations to kasher metal vessels by hagala or libun, one must continue the accepted custom. In addition, we have learned that the Sages enacted many enactments to fortify the separation between meat and dairy and to prevent a person from stumbling. Therefore they forbade eating meat and dairy together even when they are not cooked, and they even forbade eating dairy after meat, and likewise forbade eating meat at a table on which there is dairy or vice versa, and they even forbade baking dairy or meat bread lest people mistakenly eat it with the other kind (above 25:3-5; 26:1-2). It can be said that it follows from these enactments that one should not use the same vessels for meat and dairy, nor non-kosher vessels for kosher foods, and that one should be careful about all the laws of kashering that applied to metal vessels that expelled tastes also with metal vessels that do not expel tastes. For if people are not careful about this, there is concern that they will cook kosher foods in non-kosher vessels that are not clean, and will come to cook dairy in meat vessels that are not clean, or vice versa, and will transgress the prohibition of meat and milk.

In summary: the opinion of the overwhelming majority of rabbis is that even after it has become clear that metal vessels do not absorb and expel tastes, the obligation to kasher them remains in force, both because of the importance of preserving the tradition, and because of the principle we have learned from all the enactments of the Sages, that one must fortify the separation between meat and dairy and between non-kosher and kosher in order to prevent stumbling.8

notes_en.en: At first glance, since the prohibition depends on the taste absorbed in the vessel, if non-kosher food was cooked in the metal and glass vessels of our day, they do not become forbidden, since they did not absorb any taste (see SA 99:7; 122:5). And we find a precedent for this in the words of the Rishonim who were lenient in kashering glass vessels by rinsing after they were used with non-kosher food or ḥametz. And so wrote Rav Dov Lior in Devar Ḥevron YD 2:153 regarding stainless steel vessels, and he even inclined to be lenient in this ab initio if other rabbis would agree. And so wrote Rav Sitton (Ha-ma'ayan 205).

Some wished to require the continued observance of all the laws of kashering metal vessels, between dairy and meat and between forbidden and permitted, solely on the basis of tradition, which should not be changed so as not to breach the fences of halakhic observance. It is better to base it on the important halakhic principle of preserving the separation between non-kosher and kosher and between meat and dairy, a principle that rests on all the many enactments concerning the separation between meat and dairy. And we likewise find that the Sages ruled that one should not rely on people remembering to clean vessels as required (Ḥullin 8b; Rashba, Torat Ha-bayit 4:1; and see Harḥavot). But if this is the only reason, one could say that only ab initio must the separation be maintained, but if dairy was mistakenly cooked in a meat pot, it need not be kashered by hagala (and this is the opinion of Rav Naḥum Rabinovitch, Teḥumin 34, p. 126). However, it appears that since the separation of meat and dairy vessels is fundamentally based on the principles of halakha, even after the fact one must observe all the laws of kashering according to the tradition, in order to fortify the separation. This can be learned from the opinion of the Rambam and those who share his view, who held that glass vessels must be purged like metal vessels, even though it is reasonable that they knew that they do not absorb and expel, as explained in halakha 5. Similarly, it was reported in the name of Rav Shlomo Zalman Auerbach that he said that although by the basic law it seems one may be lenient, in practice one should be stringent, and only in a pressing situation did he combine this consideration toward permitting (see Teḥumin 34, p. 124, note 34).
Perhaps another principle can be added: since the vessels absorb a minute absorption, even though its taste cannot be perceived, one should not cook in them, since "one may not nullify a prohibition ab initio"; and therefore it is a mitzva to kasher vessels in which non-kosher food was cooked, because of the minute absorption they absorbed (see Harḥavot).

sections.title_en: Explanation of the Obligation to Purge Metal and Glass Vessels
sections.body_en:
Beyond what we learned in the previous section on the strength of custom and preserving the separation, it appears that also according to the principles of halakha, the obligation to kasher metal vessels remains in force without change. For we have learned that according to many, the Torah obligation to kasher vessels applies only during the first day, because then the tastes absorbed in and stuck to the vessel are still good. But after a full day these tastes become spoiled, and they no longer have the power to render forbidden the dish that will be cooked in the pot; and nevertheless the Sages established that since initially the tastes in the vessel were good, even after they have spoiled it is forbidden to use the vessel without kashering it according to the manner of its use (above halakha 3). Similarly today, even after the vessels have been cleaned well with soap, they must be kashered by rabbinic law.9

And according to the Rishonim and Aḥaronim who hold that even after a full day the obligation of kashering is by Torah law even though the tastes in the vessel are spoiled, a vessel that was cleaned well with soap also requires kashering by Torah law. And this accords with the plain meaning of the verse: "everything that may go through fire you shall pass through fire… and all that may not go through fire you shall pass through water." That is, any pot in which non-kosher food was cooked is forbidden for use as long as it has not been kashered by hagala, and anything used with fire is forbidden for use as long as it has not been kashered by libun. And this also emerges from the approach of the many Rishonim who hold that 'ta'am ke-ikar' (taste is like the substance itself) is rabbinic (as explained in the note).10

notes_en.en: According to the approach of R. Shimon, which was accepted as halakha, and as many of the Rishonim and Aḥaronim explained it (according to their version of the Gemara, Avoda Zara 76a), a spoiled taste coming out of vessels that are not ben yomam does not render forbidden, and therefore the obligation to kasher the vessels of Midian was at the time when they were ben yomam from the cooking of the non-Jews, and only by rabbinic law is it forbidden to cook in vessels that are not ben yomam, lest people come to cook in them while they are ben yomam (Avoda Zara 76a). And so it was ruled in SA 122:2 (see note 3). Accordingly, that same enactment of the Sages, which established that it is forbidden to use a vessel that is not ben yomo as long as it has not been kashered according to the manner of its use, also applies to any vessel that was cleaned well with soap: it is forbidden to use it without kashering according to the manner of its use.

To explain the approach of those who hold that the obligation of kashering is by Torah law, we must first note that there is a difficulty with the accepted approach: simply understood, the warriors returned from the war of Midian to the Israelite camp on the day after the battle, and by then the vessels were no longer ben yomam, and consequently they did not require kashering by Torah law; so why were the Israelites commanded to kasher them? And even if they returned on the same day, there is a rule: ordinary vessels are not ben yomam; so why were they commanded to kasher them? And even if we are speaking of pots that were looted while still hot, so that it was known that a full day had not passed since the non-Jews' cooking, why did the Torah command them to take the trouble to kasher them? Let it command them to wait until a full day passes, and thereby they would become fit! (And see Avoda Zara 67b, where from the plain sense of the prohibition of non-Jews' vessels requiring hagala (gi'ulei goyim), which are forbidden even after a day, R. Meir learned that noten ta'am li-fgam renders forbidden.) The Rishonim and Aḥaronim resolved this difficulty in various ways, and the difficulty still remains very strong (see Harḥavot).
The explanation that settles the matter is in accordance with the plain meaning of the verses: the obligation to kasher vessels is a scriptural decree unrelated to the taste they expel, and therefore it is binding by Torah law even when the vessels are not ben yomam, for the Torah decreed that vessels in which non-kosher foods were cooked must be kashered by hagala or libun. And this emerges from the opinion of those who hold that ta'am ke-ikar is rabbinic. For in their opinion the taste coming out of the vessel does not render forbidden by Torah law; if so, why did the Torah require kashering the vessels of Midian? Rather, one must say that the obligation of kashering does not depend on the taste coming out of the vessel. As the Ra'ah explained in the name of the Ramban (Bedek Ha-bayit 4:1), the mitzva of kashering vessels (by hagala or libun) is similar to the immersion of vessels, "because of an elevated status (ma'ala)." For it is an elevated status of the food vessels of Jews that they require immersion and kashering: if they belonged to a non-Jew, they require immersion like the immersion of a convert, and if they were used with non-kosher food, they require kashering according to the manner of their use. Thus there is an intrinsic obligation to kasher vessels in which non-kosher food was cooked, unrelated to the expulsion of the prohibition. And so wrote Rabbeinu Simḥa (cited in Responsa Maharaḥ Or Zaru'a 63) and the Pleti 98:2. If so, it appears that all those who hold that ta'am ke-ikar is rabbinic would require kashering by Torah law even of vessels that were cleaned with soap. They are: Rambam, Ramban, Ra'ah, Ran, Nimukei Yosef, Ritva (below 34, note 2). The Rashba wrote that the ruling according to the opinion that 'ta'am ke-ikar is by Torah law' is only because a doubt regarding Torah law is resolved stringently. If so, when a stringency results from the opinion of those who hold that 'ta'am ke-ikar is rabbinic,' according to whom there is a Torah obligation to kasher metal and glass vessels in which non-kosher food was cooked, one must be stringent in accordance with them. (Similarly explained the Pri Megadim 93, Siftei Da'at 3; Or Same'aḥ, Hilkhot Ma'akhalot Asurot 9:9, as explained in Harḥavot.) Likewise, in Responsa Mishneh Sakhir 2:146 (by Rav Teichtal, may God avenge his blood), he wrote that the wording of the verse implies that there is an intrinsic mitzva to kasher vessels, and not only because of the taste in them, and he therefore wondered why no blessing was instituted for it. And so explained Rav Yosef Dov Soloveitchik (Shiurei Ha-Rav §70), that the mitzva of kashering vessels stands on its own, even when the vessels contain no forbidden taste. And it appears that this should be learned from the opinion of the Rishonim who were stringent regarding glass vessels, that they cannot be kashered at all, since their law is like that of earthenware vessels (as explained in halakha 5). And it is reasonable that they too agree that glass vessels do not absorb taste; thus they were forbidden not because of absorption but because of a scriptural decree. All this is according to R. Shimon, who was accepted as halakha according to most Rishonim. In addition, according to the Sages (Pesaḥim 44b, as cited above in note 3), even though noten ta'am li-fgam does not render forbidden, the obligation to kasher vessels is a novelty and decree established by the Torah, and therefore even when the vessels are not ben yomam there is a Torah obligation to kasher them. And we found two Rishonim who ruled according to the Sages: the Ri, cited in Responsa Maharam of Rothenburg 4:213, and R. Efrayim of Regensburg, cited in Ha-manhig, p. 659. And it appears that in their opinion there is also a Torah obligation to kasher vessels in which non-kosher food was cooked even though they did not absorb tastes into them.
However, what I have explained is difficult in light of the Rishonim and the SA (451:26), who were lenient with glass vessels and did not require them to be kashered. But if we explain that their entire leniency was with a keli sheni (as explained in note 5), then they too would agree to everything I have written regarding a keli rishon. It is also possible that regarding glass vessels, which the Torah did not explicitly decree must be kashered, one may discuss exempting them from kashering when it is known that the taste has been removed from them; but metal vessels, which the Torah decreed must be kashered, must be kashered by rabbinic or Torah law even when there is no concern of a forbidden taste in them. And as the Ramban wrote, it is an elevated status of the food vessels of Jews that they require immersion and kashering; consequently, just as the immersion of glass vessels is not by Torah law (above 31:2), so one can say that the Torah also did not command the kashering of glass vessels.
At first glance, all that I have explained, that the obligation to kasher vessels is by the essential law, applies only to vessels in which non-kosher food was cooked, whereas the obligation to kasher metal vessels between meat and dairy is only because of tradition and preserving the separation between meat and dairy, as cited in the previous halakha. But one can say that the obligation of kashering between meat and dairy also remains in force as a rabbinic enactment, for we find that in many halakhot the Sages made their laws equivalent (as we learned above 29:1), and since the obligation to kasher a vessel that was used with non-kosher food has not moved from its place, the obligation of kashering between meat and dairy also remains in place.

sections.title_en: Practical Halakha for Metal and Glass Vessels
sections.body_en:
The upshot of all we have learned is that even after metal vessels are cleaned with soap, the obligation to kasher vessels in which non-kosher food was cooked remains in force. Likewise, one must kasher a meat vessel in which dairy was cooked, or vice versa. And the law of glass vessels is like the law of metal vessels (above halakha 5).

However, where the poskim disagree whether one must be concerned about taste expelled from vessels, as long as we know that the metal or glass vessels were cleaned well with soap, one should rule according to the lenient opinion. So it is regarding the law of notein ta'am bar notein ta'am (a secondary taste), and so regarding the law of a sharp food, as explained below (halakhot 11-12). For one must say that the entire dispute of the poskim concerns earthenware vessels, which soak up tastes, or metal and glass vessels that were not cleaned well with soap; but regarding metal and glass vessels that were cleaned well with soap, all would agree that the halakha follows the lenient opinion, since we know that they do not expel tastes.11

notes_en.en:
Likewise, if someone mistakenly baked meat in a clean dairy baking pan, or vice versa, the pan can be kashered by hagala or by light libun, in accordance with the law of 'it absorbed something permitted' (hetera bala) (below 33:9). Likewise, regarding whether one must wait a full day before purging the vessel (below 33:5), if the vessel was cleaned well, one should rule according to those who permit.
If a non-kosher metal pot was cleaned well with soap, and on the same day food was cooked in it, it appears that even when there was no non-Jew there who checked the dish and said that it has no non-kosher taste, after the fact the dish is kosher, since it is clear to us that it has no non-kosher taste. Likewise, if a meat metal pot was cleaned well with soap and on the same day someone mistakenly cooked dairy in it, although the pot requires kashering, the dairy that was mistakenly cooked in it is kosher, since in practice it did not receive a meat taste. Likewise, if someone mistakenly baked meat in a clean dairy baking pan that was ben yoma, although the pan requires kashering, the meat baked in it is kosher, since in practice it did not receive a dairy taste. Many are indeed accustomed to rule that as long as the vessel was ben yomo the food is forbidden, either because this is the tradition of halakhic ruling and it should not be changed, or because of the concern that perhaps the vessel was not cleaned well. However, it appears that since we know that whenever it is cleaned in the usual way with soap no taste is perceived, one should permit after the fact. Seemingly one could object: we permit on the basis of taste only when a kafila (a non-Jewish expert) checked and found that the dish has no non-kosher taste, and today the custom is not to rely on taste and not to ask a kafila (below 34:4-5); if so, how can we permit after the fact on the basis of our knowledge that there is no taste? But the whole custom of being stringent and not relying on a kafila applies in a case where there is an element of doubt; but when it is as clear as the noonday sun that the food has no forbidden taste, there is no need for a kafila. This is similar to what was written in Responsa Rema 54; Ḥatam Sofer YD 117; Maharsham 3:377. And as I wrote in note 6, hundreds of men and women checked this, and not one was found who cleaned in the usual way and perceived in the dish the taste of the previous dish.
However, if the one who cooked knew that the pot required kashering and nevertheless transgressed and cooked in it, even if the pot was cleaned with soap, the dish is forbidden to the cook and to all those for whom he cooked, just as the Sages penalized one who transgressed and cooked in a non-kosher pot over which a full day had passed. Others may eat from the dish, since in practice it contains no forbidden taste (above halakha 3).

sections.body_en:
All other vessels that are not made of metal or glass are liable to absorb and expel tastes, and therefore all the laws that depend on the expulsion of tastes from vessels apply to them, and all the disputes that depend on the expulsion of tastes, such as notein ta'am bar notein ta'am and sharp foods, apply to them. This is the law of vessels of wood, bone, leather, earthenware and plastic. A Teflon frying pan, which is composed of metal and plastic, is also included among the vessels that absorb and expel tastes.

The law of enamel vessels is like that of metal vessels; for although the enamel layer is made from sand, in practice it is hard and impermeable like glass.12

Earthenware vessels are unique: since they are full of pores and absorb many tastes, hagala and libun cannot extract from them all the taste they absorbed, and therefore if they became non-kosher there is no way to kasher them. The same is the law of clay and ceramic vessels, whose composition is similar to earthenware (above halakha 4).

It follows that the law of vessels in which non-kosher food was cooked divides into three types of vessels: a) Metal and glass vessels – the tastes stick to their walls but are not absorbed into the interior of the metal and glass; therefore, although they require kashering like all vessels, in all the laws that depend on the expulsion of taste one should rule according to the lenient opinion. b) Vessels of bone, wood, leather and ordinary plastic – they absorb and expel tastes, and in addition to requiring kashering, all the laws that depend on the expulsion of taste apply to them. c) Earthenware vessels of all kinds – they absorb and expel tastes like the vessels in the previous clause, and they have an additional stringency: if they became non-kosher there is no possibility of kashering them (halakha 4).

Porcelain (china) vessels should not, ab initio, be kashered, like earthenware vessels. In a time of need, if their glaze is smooth and impermeable and without cracks, they can be kashered by hagala like glass vessels (Peninei Halakha: Pesaḥ 11:13, note 11).13

notes_en.en:
According to Igrot Moshe (OḤ 2:92), one should not kasher by hagala plastic vessels and other vessels made from chemical materials that were not mentioned by the Rishonim, lest their law be like that of earthenware vessels, which do not expel in the way they absorbed; and this is the opinion of Rav Yosef Shalom Elyashiv and Le-horot Natan 6:69. But most poskim agreed that they can be kashered by hagala, among them: Ḥelkat Ya'akov 2:163; Seridei Esh 2:160; Rav Levi Yitzḥak Halperin; Rav Eliyahu in Hilkhot Ḥagim 5:86; Ḥazon Ovadia, Pesaḥ, p. 151; Or Le-Tzion vol. 3, 10:13. All this applies to the plastic vessels common in our day (with some types of plastic it is also dangerous to heat foods, because they release plastic residues into the food). However, since 'plastic' is a collective name for very many types of materials, it is likely that in the near future there will be plastic vessels that are impermeable like glass and metal.
Enamel vessels are made of metal and coated with a thin layer of enamel to beautify them. The inner side of the pot is usually colored white, and the outer side is decorated with various colors. Enamel is produced from sand like glass vessels, but the method of processing it is different. At first they were in doubt about the law of enamel, because the craftsmen kept its composition secret. After it became clear that its basis is sand, a doubt arose lest its law be like that of earthenware vessels. According to the Ḥatam Sofer (YD 113), it is kashered by light libun. Rabbi Shlomo Kluger (Tuv Ta'am Va-da'at, Mahadura Kamma 183) was stringent not to kasher it even by libun, lest the libun damage it. According to the Arukh Ha-shulḥan YD 121:27, it is kashered by hagala three times, relying on the opinion of the author of the Ittur (above note 4). As a matter of halakha, the accepted ruling is that they are kashered by hagala, since they are essentially metal and the enamel coating is like glass. And this is the opinion of the Aderet, Rav Eliyahu in Hilkhot Ḥagim 5:39, and Ḥazon Ovadia, Pesaḥ, p. 157.

The poskim disagree about porcelain vessels, which are also called china or 'farfuri' vessels. They are made like earthenware vessels, except that they are coated with glass, by brushing or dipping in the material from which glass is made. The Radbaz (3:401) wrote that it is proper to be stringent and regard them as earthenware vessels, since it is hard to know whether their glaze is impermeable; and he even conducted an experiment, cooking in a porcelain vessel, and found that the weight of the vessel increased slightly, which implies that it absorbed into itself. Many took his words into account, among them: Pri Ḥadash 451:26; Maḥazik Berakha 451:10; MB 451:163; Ben Ish Ḥai, Tzav 14; R. Ḥayim Palagi in Mo'ed Le-khol Ḥai 4:3; Kol Mevaser 1:80. On the other hand, many customarily were lenient and regarded it as glass. And so several poskim ruled, among them the Knesset Ha-gedola OḤ 451, Hagahot Beit Yosef 30 (and although he was stringent for himself, he in no way agreed to be stringent for others), and She'ilat Ya'avetz 1:67. And so Rav Goren ruled for the IDF regarding china plates without cracks whose manner of use is as a keli sheni (Meshiv Milḥama 2:150). Apparently, the main reason of the stringent authorities is the concern that the glassy glaze is not complete, as emerges from the Pri Ḥadash and Ḥida, that if the porcelain were genuine there would be room to be lenient, but it is commonly counterfeited. Indeed, in the past many coated earthenware with a glassy material by means of a brush or heat, and sometimes the coating was not complete and had cracks. But when the earthenware is dipped into liquid glass, the coating is uniform, smooth and strong. Therefore, although ab initio one should take into account the stringent opinion, in a time of need one may be lenient, since today high-quality porcelain and china vessels are manufactured in factories, that is, coated with glass that does not absorb. After the fact, if it was not kashered and food was unintentionally cooked in it, it is kosher. However, when there are cracks in the vessel, its law reverts to that of an earthenware vessel.
Today there are high-quality plates produced from sand (Arcopal and the like), whose texture is hard like glass, and as is evident when they break, their inner material is impermeable and hard like glass. And although for the sake of beauty their surfaces are made rough, their law is like that of glass vessels, which are kashered by hagala.

sections.title_en: Using Meat Vessels for Pareve – Notein Ta'am Bar Notein Ta'am
sections.body_en:
Some say that it is permitted ab initio to cook pareve food in a meat vessel in order to eat it with dairy, and vice versa (the custom of some of those of Sephardic descent). And some say that if the meat vessel is ben yomo it is forbidden, and if it is not ben yomo it is permitted (the custom of most of those of Sephardic descent). And some say that even in a meat vessel that is not ben yomo one should not cook pareve food in order to eat it with dairy, and only if it was already cooked and there is a need, is it permitted to mix it with dairy. But if it was cooked in a meat vessel that is ben yomo, even in a time of need it is forbidden to mix it, and if it was mistakenly mixed with dairy, it is permitted to eat it (the custom of those of Ashkenazic descent).

These differences of custom were stated regarding all vessels, but it appears that today they apply to earthenware and wooden vessels, which absorb tastes into themselves, and likewise to metal and glass vessels that were not cleaned in the way that is customary in our day. But with metal and glass vessels that were cleaned with soap as is customary in our day, since it is known that they do not expel any taste, it is reasonable that even the stringent authorities would agree with the lenient opinion, and therefore members of all communities may follow the lenient opinion, to cook pareve food in a clean meat vessel in order to eat it with dairy, and vice versa. However, we have learned (above 25:8) that as a rule one should maintain the separation between the sets of meat and dairy vessels, and when one intends to eat pareve foods with meat, it is proper to cook them in a meat pot, and when one intends to eat them with dairy, it is proper to cook them in a dairy pot. But in a time of need, and even for a minor need, it is permitted to cook a pareve dish in a clean meat vessel that is ben yomo, of metal or glass, in order to eat it with dairy, or vice versa.14

notes_en.en:
Notein ta'am bar notein ta'am of a prohibition: An earthenware pot in which non-kosher meat was cooked becomes saturated with non-kosher taste, and even if it is cleaned well, if a kosher dish is cooked in it while it is ben yoma, the dish becomes forbidden because of the non-kosher taste that came out of the pot and was absorbed in it. This is called 'notein ta'am bar notein ta'am' (abbreviated nat bar nat) of a prohibition; notein ta'am means 'imparting taste,' and nat bar nat means 'a taste imparted by an imparted taste.' That is: the non-kosher dish is the prohibition itself, and the taste absorbed from it in the pot is called notein ta'am, for it has no forbidden substance but only forbidden taste. And the taste coming out of the pot into the dish cooked in it is already a second taste – notein ta'am bar notein ta'am. The halakha is that since the taste was originally forbidden, even though it was weakened twice and reached the level of notein ta'am bar notein ta'am, the force of the prohibition still remains in it, and therefore the dish is non-kosher.
Notein ta'am bar notein ta'am of something permitted: It is explained in Ḥullin 111b: "Fish that were placed in a (meat) dish… Shmuel said: it is permitted to eat them with kutaḥ" (a dairy dip). And so is the halakha. According to the Rivan in the name of Rashi, only if the hot fish were placed on a cold meat dish is the meat taste absorbed in them considered weak, and it is permitted to eat them with dairy; but if they were cooked in a meat pot, they are considered meat, and it is forbidden to eat them with dairy. According to Sefer Ha-teruma and the Rosh, notein ta'am bar notein ta'am is still considered like the original taste, and therefore it is forbidden to eat dairy with fish that were roasted in a meat pot; but it is permitted to eat dairy with fish that were cooked in a meat pot, because they are a third-degree taste of meat, since in their opinion the cooking liquids are notein ta'am bar notein ta'am and the fish are a third-degree taste. According to most Rishonim, whether the fish were cooked or roasted in a meat pot, it is permitted to eat them with dairy, since they are notein ta'am bar notein ta'am of something permitted, and with something permitted we are not concerned about such a weak taste. So wrote the Rambam, Rashba, Ran, Rabbeinu Tam, Ri, Ra'avya and others. And so it was ruled in SA 95:1-2. The Rema was stringent ab initio like the Rivan, not to eat notein ta'am bar notein ta'am with the other kind, but after the fact, if they were mixed, he was lenient in accordance with the opinion of most poskim.
In practice there are three opinions: a) The custom of some of those of Sephardic descent, based on R. Yosef Karo in Bedek Ha-bayit: it is permitted ab initio to cook a pareve dish in a meat vessel that is ben yomo in order to eat it with dairy; and so wrote Responsa Ḥut Ha-meshulash, and Yabi'a Omer 9, YD 4, based on several Sephardic poskim. b) The custom of most of those of Sephardic descent, based on Rabbeinu Yeruḥam and the Semak: the whole permission to eat the fish with dairy is after the fact, once they have already been cooked in a meat vessel that is ben yomo; but ab initio one should not prepare a pareve dish in such a meat vessel in order to eat it with dairy, and likewise vice versa. And so it is implied by SA 95:1. And so ruled most Sephardic poskim, among them: Knesset Ha-gedola, Pri Ḥadash, Erekh Ha-shulḥan, Pri To'ar; Ben Ish Ḥai, Year 2, Koraḥ 13; Kaf Ha-ḥayim 1; Shemesh U-magen 2, YD 42-43. But if the meat pot is not ben yoma, one may cook pareve food in it in order to eat it with dairy. c) According to the custom of those of Ashkenazic descent, based on Rashi and the Rivan: even in a time of need one does not eat pareve food cooked in a meat pot that is ben yoma with dairy, and only after the fact, if they were mixed, is it permitted to eat them. But the pareve dish by itself may be eaten ab initio with dairy utensils (Rema 95:2). And if the pareve dish was cooked in a meat pot that is not ben yoma, in a time of need it is permitted to eat it with dairy (Rema 95:2; Ḥokhmat Adam 48:2). But ab initio one should not cook it for that purpose. And some are lenient in this even ab initio (Gra 95:10). But with roasting or baking, where more authorities are stringent (Sefer Ha-teruma, Rosh and Rashal), one should not be lenient.
Their dispute applies today to vessels of earthenware, wood and the like, which do not become thoroughly clean; but if one cooked in metal and glass vessels that were cleaned with soap as is customary in our day, according to what was explained above in halakhot 7-9, members of all communities may follow the lenient opinion, since it is known that the vessels do not expel tastes. However, ab initio, in order to maintain the separation between meat and dairy, the practice is as explained above.

sections.title_en: A Sharp Pareve Food Cooked or Cut with a Meat Vessel
sections.body_en:
A sharp food is a food that one does not usually eat by itself because of its great pungency, such as garlic, onion and hot pepper. The Rishonim disagreed about the law of a sharp pareve food that was cooked in a meat or dairy vessel. Some say that the sharpness intensifies the tastes in the vessel, and thereby the sharp food soaks up the meat taste and becomes meat. Likewise regarding a meat knife with which a sharp food was cut: since it is pressed forcefully into the food, by virtue of the food's sharpness it causes the meat taste to be absorbed in the food, which becomes meat. And some say that only when the vessels were not cleaned well is there an extra stringency in the laws of sharp foods; but if they were cleaned properly, their law is like that of a food that is not sharp, which does not absorb meat taste when it is cooked in a meat pot or when it is cut with a meat knife.

In practice, when the metal and glass vessels were cleaned properly with soap, since we know that they do not expel any taste, one should rule according to the lenient opinion: even if a sharp food was cooked in a clean meat or dairy vessel, or a sharp food was cut with a clean meat or dairy knife, the sharp food remains pareve and it is permitted to eat it with the other kind.15

notes_en.en:
A sharp food and a knife: The Sages said that if a very sharp radish was cut with a meat knife, it is forbidden to eat the radish with dairy (Ḥullin 111b). And so is the law for every sharp food, that is, a food that people do not usually eat by itself because of its great pungency, such as onion, garlic, hot pepper and horseradish (SA 96:2; according to Rabbeinu Yeḥiel the law is so only with ḥiltit (asafoetida) and radish, and his opinion has been combined for leniency, as cited in Shakh 96:12). That is, although usually tastes pass from a vessel to food only through cooking, here, where there is a combination of sharpness with the pressure of the knife, even though the sharp food is cold, the taste coming out of the knife is absorbed in the sharp food. Some say that the intent is the meat fat on the knife, which through the pressure of the knife is absorbed in the sharp food; but if the knife is clean (as was customary in the past), the sharp food remains pareve (first explanation in Rashi, Ramban, Nimukei Yosef, Rashba, Ra'ah, Orḥot Ḥayim, Ran, Ritva, Me'iri, and this is the opinion of the Rif and Rambam according to the Beit Yosef). And so wrote in practice the Pri Ḥadash 96:2 and Avnei Tzedek. And the Pleti 1 and Responsa Makom Shmuel 89 inclined to this. And some say that even when the meat knife is clean (as was customary in the past), when an onion is cut with it, through the pressure and the sharpness, the meat taste absorbed in the knife will come out and be absorbed in the onion (second explanation in Rashi, Sefer Ha-teruma, Rosh, Ra'avya, Or Zaru'a, and so it is implied by Rabbeinu Tam and the Mordekhai). And so ruled the Shulḥan Arukh (96:1) and most Aḥaronim, among them: Shakh, Gra, Pri To'ar, Ḥavot Da'at, Pri Megadim and Ḥokhmat Adam. The Rema (96:3), based on Sefer Ha-teruma and several Rishonim, added a further stringency, that even if the knife is not ben yoma the onion becomes meat, because the sharpness turns the spoiled meat taste in the knife into a good taste.
To what extent is the taste of the knife absorbed in the sharp food? Some say to the depth of a peel (kedei klipa) (Rosh and Rabbeinu Yeruḥam). And some say to the depth of a netila, about two cm (1.9 cm) (Ra'avad, Ra'ah, Semag, SA 96:1, and others). And some say throughout the entire food (Rashba and Ran, and the Rema took their approach into account ab initio). The SA (96:1) wrote that if a Jew tasted the sharp food and found that it had no meat taste from the knife, it remains pareve. And according to the Yam Shel Shlomo, Shakh 96:5 and others, ab initio one should not rely on tasting.
A sharp food and cooking: In principle, the dispute about a knife and a sharp food also applies to a sharp cooked dish; and just as regarding a knife the SA and Rema ruled according to the stringent opinion, so regarding a very sharp pareve dish, such as sḥug, which is made mainly of hot pepper, that was cooked in a clean meat pot that is ben yoma, they ruled that the dish is meat, because its sharpness turns the notein ta'am bar notein ta'am of meat into an actual meat taste, and therefore it is forbidden to eat it with dairy. And if it was mixed into a dairy dish and the dairy dish did not contain sixty times its amount, everything is forbidden. But if the meat pot is not ben yoma, according to the main opinion in the SA, since the meat taste absorbed in it is spoiled, the sharp dish remains pareve. And according to the Rema, even when the pot is not ben yoma the dish becomes meat, because the sharpness of the food turns the spoiled taste into a good one (see SA 96:1; Rema 95:2).
All this is according to the state of cleanliness of knives and metal pots in the past, when the metals were generally rougher and less polished, and they were cleaned without soap and without running water in the home, so that even after cleaning off the visible fat on the vessel, a certain greasiness from the dish cooked or cut with them often remained stuck to the vessels, leaving a faint trace, and this is what is called notein ta'am bar notein ta'am. When it met a sharp food, its taste was intensified slightly, to the point that sometimes some trace of it was noticeable. The Rishonim disagreed whether this trace should be taken into account to turn the pareve food into meat or dairy. But in our day it is clear that after metal knives and pots are cleaned with a scouring cloth with water and soap, they do not expel any taste, and consequently the foods cut or cooked with them remain pareve. This is clear according to the opinion of the lenient authorities, who ruled so even after the cleaning that was customary in the past (first explanation in Rashi, Ramban, Nimukei Yosef, Rashba, Ra'ah, Orḥot Ḥayim, Ran, Ritva, Me'iri, and this is the opinion of the Rif and Rambam according to the Beit Yosef). And even according to the stringent authorities, who hold that knives and pots that were cleaned according to the custom of the past may expel tastes and turn pareve foods into meat (second explanation in Rashi, Sefer Ha-teruma, Rosh, Ra'avya, Or Zaru'a, and so it is implied by Rabbeinu Tam and the Mordekhai, and the SA, Rema and most Aḥaronim), when it is known to all that in practice knives and metal pots that were cleaned well with soap as is customary in our day do not expel tastes, one should be lenient and regard sharp pareve foods that were cut or cooked with meat knives and pots as pareve. This is clear according to the SA (96:1), who wrote that if they tasted the onion and did not perceive the meat taste, it remains pareve. And even according to those who hold that ab initio one does not rely on a taste test regarding a particular food about which a doubt arose, when everyone knows clearly, like the noonday sun, that one never perceives a taste coming out of clean knives and pots, we rely on this without needing to check the taste of each and every food (see Responsa Rema 54; Ḥatam Sofer YD 117; Maharsham 3:377; and as above in note 11). It follows that if it is known that the meat knife and pots were clean, even though pareve foods were cut and cooked with them, they remain pareve.
Likewise, if sharp spices were ground in a grinder in which hot meat was ground on the same day, if the grinder was made of metal and was cleaned well, the spices remain pareve (the words of the SA 96:3 refer to a case where they could not clean the mortar well. However, when the mortar is made of stone or wood, one should be stringent).

sections.body_en:
A cutting board made of wood or plastic is liable to soak up tastes, because its material absorbs tastes, and also because cutting creates cuts in it in which tastes are absorbed. Therefore, one should designate a cutting board for meat foods and a cutting board for dairy foods. One who wishes to cut foods for both kinds should designate a cutting board for pareve foods. However, after the fact, if vegetables were cut on a meat cutting board that was cleaned well, and they were mixed into a dairy dish, the dish is kosher.

When sharp foods such as onion and garlic are cut on the cutting board, because of their sharpness, when they are pressed against the board they are liable to soak up more tastes, to the point that some hold that if the board is meat they become meat, and if dairy they become dairy (Ḥokhmat Adam 56:2). Ab initio one should take their opinion into account; and if an onion was cut on a clean dairy cutting board, and it was mistakenly mixed into a meat dish that did not contain sixty times the onion, the meat dish should be forbidden to eat, lest a dairy taste entered it by way of the onion. In a pressing situation, as long as it is reasonable that the dairy taste cannot be perceived in the meat dish, the dish may be declared kosher.

A cutting board made of glass or metal does not absorb and expel tastes, and therefore, even if it is meat or dairy, if it was cleaned properly, it may be used for cutting pareve foods, even sharp ones, for the other kind.16

notes_en.en: A cutting board: Sometimes the board becomes meat or dairy, for example if scalding meat or scalding cheese foods were cut on it. The Ḥokhmat Adam 56:2 introduced the novel ruling that the law of the surface one cuts on is like the law of the knife: since the sharp food is pressed against it, if it is meat, the sharp food cut on it becomes meat. And so wrote Tuv Ta'am Va-da'at 3:216. On the other hand, according to Sefer Yehoshua (Psakim U-khtavim 122) and Ḥavalim Ba-ne'imim, since the pressure of the surface is not as strong as the pressure of the knife, the surface does not cause its taste to be absorbed in the sharp food. Ab initio we take into account the stringent opinion, and as long as the wooden or plastic cutting board is meat, the sharp food cut on it is meat, and if it was mixed into a dairy dish that did not contain sixty times its amount, the dish is forbidden. However, in a pressing situation one may rely on the lenient authorities, since in practice one generally does not perceive an actual meat taste in the onion. And one should combine the opinion of the Ra'avad and Rid, who hold that one estimates the percentage of meat that could be in the onion, as several poskim wrote that their approach may be combined to create a double doubt (above note 2). And if the food cut there was not finely chopped, one may combine the opinion of those who hold (Rosh and Rabbeinu Yeruḥam) that it is absorbed in the food only to the depth of a peel.

sections.title_en: A Spoon and the Wall of a Pot
sections.body_en:
It is forbidden to stir a meat dish with a dairy metal spoon, and likewise it is forbidden to stir a dairy dish with a meat metal spoon. If one mistakenly stirred, if the spoon was clean, the dish is kosher, since the spoon does not expel tastes; but the spoon requires kashering by hagala, since it was used once with boiling-hot dairy and once with boiling-hot meat. (The note explains the law when the spoon was made of wood or of metal that was not clean.)17

It is forbidden to stir with a dairy spoon a pareve dish cooked in a meat pot, and likewise it is forbidden to stir with a meat spoon a pareve dish cooked in a dairy pot. But if one mistakenly stirred, the dish is kosher and the spoon does not require kashering.18

If milk fell on the outside walls of a metal pot in which meat is being cooked, the meat dish is kosher, and the pot requires kashering by hagala.19

If boiling-hot non-kosher gravy spilled on a cold kosher metal or glass pot, it is not necessary to kasher the whole pot by hagala; rather, it is sufficient to kasher it by pouring boiling water (irui) on the place where the non-kosher gravy spilled. Likewise, if boiling-hot milk spilled on a cold meat metal or glass pot, it should be kashered by pouring boiling water on the place where the milk spilled.

notes_en.en: We learned in halakhot 7-8 that a metal spoon that is clean as is customary in our day does not expel tastes, and therefore it does not render forbidden, but it itself requires kashering. But if the dairy spoon was made of wood, and the dish did not contain sixty times what entered it from the spoon, if the spoon was ben yoma, the dish becomes forbidden, and the spoon requires kashering by hagala. The law is the same if the dairy spoon was made of metal and was not cleaned properly (Sefer Ha-teruma, Semag, Semak and others). One authority is stringent to require sixty times the entire spoon, since when part of the spoon is hot the whole of it is considered hot and expels tastes (Rabbeinu Peretz). The main ruling follows the lenient opinion (SA and Rema 94:1).

If one stirred with a dairy earthenware or wooden spoon that was ben yomo a pareve dish cooked in a meat earthenware or wooden vessel that was ben yomo, and the dish did not contain sixty times the pot nor sixty times the spoon, according to SA 95:3 the dish is kosher, because it is notein ta'am bar notein ta'am of something permitted, and the vessels do not require kashering. According to the Rema the dish is forbidden, because there is concern that before it became notein ta'am bar notein ta'am of something permitted, the dairy and meat tastes became mixed together, and the vessels require kashering. And if one of the vessels was not ben yomo, the dish is permitted, and the vessels require kashering. But if one of the vessels was of metal or glass, clean as is customary in our day, it appears that even the Rema and those who share his view would agree with the SA, as explained above in halakhot 7-9. However, ab initio one should not stir with a dairy spoon pareve food that is in a meat pot, or vice versa, even if both are of metal and are not ben yomam, for this has been the custom of the Jewish people, in order to fortify the separation between meat and dairy and to prevent confusion.

Regarding vessels of other materials that absorb tastes, four main opinions were stated about the law of a drop of milk that fell on a boiling-hot meat pot. a) According to the Semag, the drop of milk can spread through all the walls of the pot, and since it spreads gradually, by the rules of ḥatikha na'aseit nevela (the piece itself becomes forbidden), it will eventually render forbidden everything absorbed in the walls of the pot; and since the dish does not contain sixty times the walls of the pot, the dish will become forbidden and the pot requires hagala. b) According to the Maharam of Rothenburg, the drop of milk can render forbidden the tastes absorbed in the wall up to sixty times its amount; then, if the dish contains sixty times sixty the drop of milk that fell on the pot, the dish is kosher. And the pot in any case requires hagala. c) According to the Semak, if the pot was uncovered and the drop fell above the level of the dish, there is concern that it will render forbidden sixty times its amount of what is absorbed in the wall opposite the drop, and therefore it is forbidden to pour out the dish by way of the place of absorption while it is still hot. But if it fell opposite the dish, or the pot was covered and completely full of hot steam, since the dish contains sixty times the drop alone, the dish is kosher; and some say that according to his approach the pot must be purged (Beit Yosef), and some say it need not (Taz). d) According to R. Yeḥiel of Paris, even if the drop fell not opposite the dish and the pot was uncovered, in a pressing situation, as long as the dish contained sixty times the drop, the dish is kosher. In practice, it was ruled in the SA and Rema 92:5-7 according to the opinion of the Semak; ab initio, when the drop fell above the level of the dish, the custom is to forbid everything, and in a pressing situation one follows the opinion of R. Yeḥiel of Paris. Whenever the pot requires hagala, if it is made of earthenware, hagala does not kasher it, as explained in halakha 4.
